title: fugaro orchestrator --json documents (ls, state, events, patch, plan_import)
description: The five documents `fugaro orchestrator ls`, `state`, `events`, `patch` and `import --plan` print with --json (the stateless-orchestrator plan's O5 and the cli-output-console-graph plan's CG4, D1223, D1358). They are the CLI's own contract with whatever reads them — the console, a session, a script — and they are additives-only under version 1: a field never changes meaning, a new one is added, and a renamed one is a new version. The state document carries the generated summary rather than the raw state, because the summary is what the state model itself calls the state as a person or a session reads it and it is capped (internal/orchestrator.Summarize), so a consumer that reads it pays a bounded cost whatever the node grew to; `rev` is the revision the node was at, which is the `base_rev` a patch built from that read carries. The listing document is the orchestrators an installation has, and it is the one that reads two things rather than one: the database's subtree and this machine's cached briefs. The events document is the audit log in the order the server stamped it, oldest first, and it is what `internal/orchestrator.Entry` marshals: the id and the stamp are the log's own, derived on append and never by the caller. The patch document reports the write that landed — which class of actor made it among them. That class is `session` or `person` and never `daemon` or `decision-agent`: no flag, environment variable or field of the document makes the CLI act as either (G1), so this enum is the fence written down. Every timestamp field the commands format themselves is second-precision UTC RFC 3339 — state's and patch's, and the listing's `updated_at` and `cached_at`; the audit's own stamps are too, because internal/orchestrator.audit's Append truncates them (stamp). The brief and the event texts carry stored text, already cleaned and, for the brief, fenced by the summary that generated it (G3).

id.description: The orchestrator id: the selected project's own orchestrator is the project's name, and one of its named orchestrators is `<project>~<name>` (C-ORCH, D3206, D3207), which a command names with `--name` and never as a whole id. The pattern is internal/orchestrator's orchestrator id rule (ParseOrchestratorID), the rule every path under orchestrator/<id> is built and checked by: the project half is config.ProjectNameRE, the separator is `~`, and the name half is 1 to 40 characters of a-z, 0-9 and `-` starting with a letter or a digit. It is not agentRE widened (F36) — a work item's id and an orchestrator's are not the same string in one keyspace — and there is no cap on how many named orchestrators a project has.

stamp.description: A second-precision UTC RFC 3339 instant. It is the database server's clock wherever it is a stamp of the state (D1230): a laptop's own clock is not what the order of the audit log, or the date of an approval, may depend on.

ls.description: The orchestrators an installation has (D1358, D1361): every id whose node exists under `orchestrator/` in the project's database, and every cached brief this machine holds. It is written on every run, empty list included, so a consumer reads it without a nil check, and the two reads behind it are what the daemon itself writes — there is no registry of processes and no port.

orchestrators.description: The orchestrators, by id. An id is one orchestrator however many places name it: one the database holds and this machine caches is a single entry, and its kind is `local`.

kind.description: Where the orchestrator is kept. `local` is one this machine runs: the daemon here wrote its cached brief. `central` is one only the project's database holds.

project.description: The orchestrator id, as it stands under `orchestrator/` in the database: the project's own orchestrator's id is the project's name, and a named one's is `<project>~<name>` (C-ORCH, D3206, D3207). The field is named `project` from when an id was always a project's name; the id is what it carries now, so a consumer that wants the project reads the part before `~`. The pattern is internal/orchestrator's orchestrator id rule, and it is written on every entry: an older CLI's document is the one that lacks the field, so an entry that does not carry it is not this release's.

name.description: The name half of the id — what `--name` takes: the slug after `~` for a named orchestrator, and the empty string for the project's own, which is a real answer and not an absent one. It is written on every entry, so a consumer can label a node without parsing the id itself, and it is never the project's name: that half of the id is `project`.

driver.description: The principal of the credential driving the orchestrator, read from its `orchestrator/<id>/driver` node (D3218, F18) — the account whose login unit or foreground run holds the id, in the address spelling the rest of the tree uses for a person (localcfg's Me). It is written on every entry, and the empty string is the honest answer for an id whose node does not exist — every orchestrator nothing has driven since the node was introduced, and every one this machine caches and the database does not hold — or whose node this release cannot read: the contract's own reading is that an empty driver is never "nobody drives this" (contract-orchestrators.md, "what each side may rely on" 2), and which of the two it is, is not a value this field can carry. Nothing is checked of a non-empty value here, which is the whole of what the node's decoder refuses (internal/orchestrator.DecodeDriver): a pattern here would be a second rule for a value this side does not mint.

lease_holder.description: The holder the id's lease node names, which is the daemon driving it. Absent when the node carries no claim, and always absent for an orchestrator this machine caches and the database does not hold.

updated_at.description: The server time of that holder's last beat, read from the lease node. Absent when there is no claim.

cached_at.description: When this machine's daemon wrote the orchestrator's cached brief — the same freshness stamp `state --brief --offline` prints. Absent for an orchestrator this machine does not run.

cache_stale.description: Whether the id this cached brief belongs to is still being driven, which is what says the brief is being rewritten: true when nothing is beating the id — no lease node at all, or a last beat older than the lease's TTL (internal/orchestrator.LeaseClaim.Fresh) — measured against the database's own clock. It is the lease's answer and not the brief's own age: a daemon beats on the lease's cadence whatever its cycles do, and a cycle that failed writes no cache. Written only when it is true, and never without cached_at.

state.$comment: A node's document carries rev and schema_version, and a cache's carries neither. It is said conditionally rather than in the fields' own descriptions because zero is a revision a live node really is at — the revision of a node nobody has written yet — so a writer that drops the field as an empty value has to fail this contract rather than pass as an absent optional.

source.description: Where the brief came from: `node` is the live state node, read over the project's database as the person's own credential; `cache` is the file the daemon writes at session start and `--brief --offline` prints, which reaches no network at all (D1243).

rev.description: The revision the state node was at, and so the `base_rev` a patch built from this read carries. It is written for `node` and never for `cache`, and an empty node's revision 0 is written too.

schema_version.description: The state document's own schema version (internal/orchestrator.SchemaVersion), written for `node`. A node saved at an older version is migrated by the reader before the summary is generated, and the next write carries the raised version.

brief.description: The generated summary: the goal, the work items with their phases, the questions waiting on someone and the facts, with every stored string fenced and cleaned and the whole of it capped by the generator (internal/orchestrator.Summarize). It is the same text `fugaro orchestrator state --brief` prints without --json.

items.description: Every work item of the live state node, uncapped and in the state's own order, so a reader never has to parse the brief's prose (which lists running items first and is capped). Written for `node` and never for `cache`, and empty when the node holds none: an empty list is omitted.

run_id.description: The run id the item's last attempt recorded; absent before any run.

spec.description: The plan folder the item declares; absent when it declares none.

cached_at.description: When the daemon wrote the cached brief, which is its freshness stamp: `--brief --offline` prints it so that a stale cache is visible rather than silent. Written for `source: cache` and never for `node`.

since.description: The cut `--since` was resolved to, on the database's own clock. Written only when --since was passed; absent means the whole log.

events.description: The audit log, oldest first by the server's stamp with the derived id breaking a tie. It is written on every run, empty included, so a consumer may read it without a nil check. An audit node that does not exist yet is an empty log rather than an error.

id.description: The derived id, `subject:transition` (internal/orchestrator.EntryID): the same event delivered twice is one entry, so a reader never sees the same thing twice.

subject.description: What the entry is about: a work item's, a decision's or a run's name (internal/orchestrator's idRE).

text.description: A short line for a person reading it later, capped by the writer (internal/orchestrator.MaxAuditTextRunes). Absent when the transition carries nothing to say; what a model said goes in the run's own record and not here.

rev.description: The revision the write landed at, one past the revision the run read: the document is a report of a write that happened, and there is no refusal here because a refusal is an error and not a document.

actor.description: Which class of actor made the write. `session` is a run that landed only what a session may land; `person` is a run that passed the typed confirmation at a real terminal, and the whole patch landed as that person. The two other classes are not here on purpose: nothing a caller passes makes this command the daemon or the decision agent.

ops.description: How many ops the document carried. The bounds are internal/orchestrator.ValidatePatch's: a patch with no op would change nothing, and one over MaxOps is refused.

plan.description: The plan's name: its folder under docs/, which is the node's own name in the orchestrator's plan shard and the spec every item the import writes carries. The pattern is internal/orchestrator's spec name rule.

commit.description: The commit the plan stands at, which every brief the import wrote pins beside the hash of its task's section (D2737). internal/orchestrator's headRE.

rev.description: The revision the plan's node stands at when the import is done. Unlike the patch document's, 0 is allowed: an import that writes no op is not a write, so it reports the node as it found it — which is 0 for a plan whose node has never been written.

ops.description: How many ops this import wrote, which is zero for a re-import of an unchanged plan (D2745). The upper bound is internal/orchestrator.MaxOps, the most a patch carries.

items.description: Every task of the graph in the graph's own order, each with the id its item stands under in the node and the digest of the spec it stands for. This is the list `plan_approve` takes and the reason the document exists: the import lands as a session and approves nothing, so a person approves these items from this list (D2706).

id.description: The work item's id in the plan's node, which is the graph's node id everywhere but where the daemon had already adopted a run for that task: an adopted item keeps its own id and the import links to it rather than writing a second item (D2746). The pattern is internal/orchestrator's idRE, which is also why a plan whose tasks are numbered with a dot cannot be imported (F37).

digest.description: The item's spec digest, the same value internal/orchestrator.SpecDigest computes and the one an approval binds.
